scenario.title: Misbehaving task hits the MPU stack guard - kernel kills it, others continue
scenario.description: Same kernel as P06, but task C starts recursing without bound after a few iterations. Each level pushes four words and never returns. The stack grows down into the 32-byte guard region below it, which the MPU marks no-access for everyone. The first push into the guard is a MemManage fault; the fault handler identifies the task from EXC_RETURN and PSP, marks it DEAD and switches to another task. A and B keep running and the UART keeps printing.

expected.summary: One MemManage fault with MMARVALID pointing into guard_C; task C is DEAD with a 100 percent watermark; A and B keep running; no lockup.

scenario.what_to_look_for: A marker event "taskC: deep recursion begins", then a fault event from context C: "MemManage at PC=... (push {r4, r5, r6, lr}): write not permitted in stack guard 'guard_C'". The fault record shows MMFSR DACCVIOL and MMARVALID, MMFAR inside guard_C: an address inside the pushed range (on the M33 typically the lowest; the model stores in ascending order, so MMFAR = C's stack_base - 16 = 0x20000270), and sp=psp equal to C's stack_base: the push was abandoned, so SP did not move. Because PSP is already at the edge, the hardware cannot push the fault frame either, so a second fault event reports a stacking error (MSTKERR, CFSR=0x00000092); the kernel still identifies C from EXC_RETURN=0xFFFFFFFD (a task was running). Run "r2s fault P07" to decode both records. Then a task_state event C -> DEAD "kernel kills the task", a context_switch to the next task, and the alphabet continues. In the summary, C's watermark is 100 percent (every word overwritten) while A and B stay around 25 percent.
likely_root_causes: Unbounded recursion or a large local array in a task with a small stack.
A task calling a library routine (printf, floating point) that needs far more stack than planned.
Stack size computed in words but passed in bytes (or the reverse), making the real stack four times smaller than intended.
how_to_debug: Read SCB->CFSR and SCB->MMFAR in the fault handler: DACCVIOL + MMARVALID with MMFAR in the guard just below a task's stack base (anywhere in the pushed range, typically its lowest address) is a stack overflow caught by the guard.
Check which stack the frame is on: EXC_RETURN bit 2 set (0xFFFFFFFD) means the task's PSP, so the faulting task is the current TCB.
Print the stack watermark of every task periodically; a task that climbs toward 100 percent is the next one to fault.
Give the task more stack or remove the recursion; keep the guard, it costs one MPU region per task.
scenario.what_this_means: Without protection a stack overflow silently corrupts whatever lies below the stack (see P09). An MPU guard region turns that silent corruption into a precise fault at the first bad write, with the address in MMFAR and the guilty task identifiable from PSP. The kernel can then contain the damage to that one task, which is the whole promise of memory protection.
scenario.hidden_symptom: One of the three tasks stops; the other two keep going; the fault log shows a MemManage with an address just below a stack.
